one_liner: Small C++20 unary-only gRPC server on nghttp2 and libuv; author's hello-world h2load runs show ~2.3-3x gRPC C++ throughput.
what_it_does: A server-only gRPC implementation that speaks the gRPC-over-HTTP/2 wire protocol over plaintext h2c, so stock gRPC clients such as grpcurl can call it, but it has its own server API. The protoc plugin protoc-gen-grpcxx emits a small header of grpcxx::rpc / grpcxx::service type aliases plus a stub ServiceImpl. You implement each method by specialising a template call<Rpc>(grpcxx::context&, const Request&) that returns {status, optional<Response>}, then add the service to grpcxx::server and call run(ip, port). Only unary calls exist: no client, streaming, TLS or compression.
how_it_is_fast: HTTP/2 framing is delegated to nghttp2 in its in-memory mode (nghttp2_session_mem_recv2 / mem_send2), driven by one libuv event loop that owns all socket I/O and wraps reads and writes in C++20 coroutines (Asio with coroutines is an optional, slower backend). Each read batch is parsed into complete requests and handed to a small mutex/condition-variable worker pool (or run inline when workers = 0). All HEADERS, DATA and trailer frames produced for that batch go into one buffer, which is flushed with a single uv_write. Dispatch is two hash lookups (service, then method) into std::function handlers, with no completion queues, call objects, interceptors, deadlines, TLS or compression on the path. No profile explaining the gap to gRPC C++ is published; PR #24 (keeping all I/O on one loop) is the change that pushed throughput past 400k req/s.
when_to_use: Internal C++ unary services whose callers are ordinary gRPC stubs in any language, with TLS terminated by a proxy or sidecar (the author suggests Envoy in issue #29).
Small request/response messages at high request rates over many multiplexed HTTP/2 connections, the shape the published benchmark measures.
Builds where the full grpc++ dependency tree and its generated code are unwanted: grpcxx needs only nghttp2, libuv (or Asio) and protobuf, and generates one short header per .proto.
Programs that already run a libuv loop or use systemd socket activation: listen() returns the uv_loop_t, run() accepts a pre-bound socket, and shutdown uses std::stop_token.
when_not_to_use: Any client, server or bidirectional streaming RPC: not supported. The streaming request (issue #49) was moved to a discussion with no implementation.
You need in-process TLS/mTLS, ALTS, compression or auth plugins (TLS issue #47 is open; issue #29 confirms none are supported), or a gRPC client (issue #48 is open; the library is server-only).

Blocking or long-running handlers. A connection stops reading while its batch runs, so requests on one connection are processed one after another. With workers = 0 a slow handler stalls the whole I/O loop. There is no async handler API, grpc-timeout deadline or cancellation.
Large messages: the libuv backend reads through a fixed 1 KiB buffer (FIXME), and every chunk makes a round trip to a worker thread. No large-payload benchmark exists.
Windows with the default libuv backend: MSVC fails to build it (C2894), so CI builds only the Asio backend on Windows.

integration.form: static lib (shared with BUILD_SHARED_LIBS); CMake project consumed via FetchContent, or find_package after install; no distro packages
integration.dependencies: nghttp2 >= 1.64.0; libuv >= 1.51.0 (default) or Asio >= 1.28 / Boost.Asio >= 1.81 (GRPCXX_USE_ASIO); Protobuf >= 3.15 (must be installed on the system); fmt >= 11.1.4 for the protoc plugin. The default GRPCXX_HERMETIC_BUILD=ON fetches libuv, nghttp2 and fmt.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20, CMake >= 3.27. Clang/AppleClang builds add -fexperimental-library for std::stop_token. CI builds GCC and Clang on Ubuntu 26.04 and macOS, plus MSVC (Asio only). Minimum compiler versions are not documented.
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (CI); Windows only with the Asio backend; no architecture-specific code (benchmarks ran on Apple M1 Max, arm64)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. From source: libuv server(n) runs I/O on one loop thread and handlers on n worker threads (default hardware_concurrency, 0 = inline on the loop). Handlers for different connections therefore run concurrently, so ServiceImpl must be thread-safe. add() the services before run(); services must outlive the server.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — wire-compatible with standard gRPC clients for unary calls over plaintext HTTP/2, but server code must be rewritten to grpcxx's template API, and there is no client, streaming, TLS, compression, interceptors or deadlines

gotchas: SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS is hard-coded to 10 per connection (FIXME in lib/grpcxx/h2/session.cpp). Clients that open more streams on one connection queue behind that limit.

Length-prefix parsing looks fragile (from reading the code; no issue filed). PR #51 masked only the last prefix byte, so bytes 1-3 still sign-extend from char on x86-64 and Apple arm64. That decodes request lengths with bit 15 or 23 set (for example 32-64 KiB) as huge values. A 5-byte prefix split across two reads is also appended incorrectly. In either case the handler can receive an empty or default request. Test with your real message sizes.

Handler exceptions derived from std::exception become INTERNAL status, including protobuf parse failures of bad input. Any other thrown type escapes a noexcept function and calls std::terminate. All grpc-* request headers (grpc-timeout, grpc-encoding) are ignored, and the compressed-flag byte is read but not used.

The test suite has no request/response round-trip test; test/uv/test_server.cpp notes testing was manual (Postman) until a client exists. Open issue #62: non-hermetic builds fail against system fmt 12.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick grpcxx over brpc when you want only a lean unary gRPC server that stock gRPC clients can call, not brpc's larger multi-protocol framework (brpc also serves h2/gRPC and adds clients, streaming RPC and load balancing). The SRPC and rest_rpc READMEs do not list gRPC wire support (SRPC lists SRPC/bRPC/Thrift/tRPC; rest_rpc has its own coroutine client), so choose them only when you control both ends. No benchmark compares grpcxx with any of the three.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran h2load (single client thread) against the unary helloworld example on an M1 Max MacBook Pro. grpcxx v0.2.0 (libuv, single-threaded) reached 452k req/s at 100 clients x 10 streams, against 142k for the gRPC C++ v1.48.4 callback server (~3.2x). The gRPC row comes from a 2023 run on a different M1 Max and macOS; the only same-machine comparison (PR #2) gives ~2.3-2.5x. Compiler and build flags are not stated for either side, and the repo's bench.sh builds through a Makefile that sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE. grpcxx's 2b and 3b cells both plateau near 450k whatever the worker count, which suggests the load generator, not the server, sets the ceiling.
status_note: Actively maintained (v0.7.0 in May 2026, last commit 2026-05-19) and MIT-licensed, but pre-1.0 with 115 stars, shipped only as source through CMake FetchContent, and with an open build break against fmt 12 in non-hermetic builds.
